cards.headline: Port St. Lucie moves forward on Midway Road expansion and new Florida Turnpike interchange
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance last month to donate 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for construction of a partial interchange on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said the interchange project aims to improve accessibility and accommodate growth in the city. "This is a way for us to try to accommodate the growth that's already occurred, but also the growth that will occur over the next 20 to 50 years," Samples said. He also noted a significant gap between current Turnpike entrances and exits in Port St. Lucie that the project will help address.

The broader Midway Road Widening Project, funded at $95 million, is currently in its first phase, which expands the roadway from two lanes to four lanes between Selvitz Road and Jenkins Road. The second phase, stretching from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road, remains in the design phase with construction expected to start in Summer 2027. FDOT also plans to construct new bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks as part of the overall project. The partial interchange remains in the design phase. City council will vote on final approval to transfer the land to FDOT at an upcoming meeting.

hero.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs jump 4% as ground beef and strawberry prices climb
hero.body:
Celebrating Independence Day with a cookout for 10 people will cost significantly more this year. According to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey, the average holiday meal now costs $73.82, representing a 4% increase from last year. The price hike reflects broader inflation pressures affecting most cookout staples, from main courses to side dishes and desserts.

Several key ingredients are driving the cost increases. Ground beef prices have risen 5.5%, while hamburger buns climbed even higher at 7.7%. Strawberries have been hit particularly hard, jumping 12.4% in price due to a Florida frost that damaged crops. Ice cream prices are also up 5.3%, making frozen desserts more expensive for holiday celebrations. These items represent some of the most popular choices for Fourth of July gatherings, putting upward pressure on typical holiday budgets.

Not all cookout items are becoming more expensive, offering some relief for budget-conscious shoppers. Potato prices have declined this year, benefiting those planning to serve potato chips or potato salad. Corn prices have been more volatile, though locally grown corn from the Glades region can provide better value for area residents. Finding these savings requires attention to what is available in local markets.

Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommended several strategies for controlling cookout costs without sacrificing quality. "It's really important to shop savvier than ever, it is comparing the stores to see who has the best deals for the groceries on your list," Woroch said. She emphasized that families should prioritize reducing food waste, which begins with planning meals in advance. By creating a detailed meal plan before shopping, consumers can avoid purchasing unnecessary items and make more strategic purchasing decisions across different retailers. These simple planning steps can help offset the inflationary pressures affecting cookout expenses this year, allowing families to celebrate the holiday while managing their food budgets more effectively.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County schools earn third straight 'A' rating with 93.5% graduation rate
cards.teaser: The School District of Palm Beach County received an 'A' rating from the state for the third consecutive year, with 84% of district-operated schools earning A or B grades.
cards.body:
The School District of Palm Beach County earned an "A" rating from the Florida Department of Education for the third consecutive year. This year, 143 district-operated schools, or 84%, received "A" or "B" ratings, an increase from 120 schools the previous year. The district also achieved a record graduation rate of 93.5%. District leaders reported that 86% of seniors participated in college-level coursework, taking at least one Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate, Cambridge Advanced International Certificate of Education, or Dual Enrollment course. Additionally, 144 recent graduates earned an associate degree alongside their high school diploma.

S.D. Spady Elementary School in Delray Beach achieved one of the district's most dramatic improvements, jumping from a "C" rating to an "A" this year. Principal Rona Tata, who has served as principal for 15 years after five years as assistant principal, led the turnaround. Three years ago, the school modified its early childhood curriculum program, which starts at age 3 and combines with kindergarten. Those students are now in third grade and performing at higher levels. Spady Elementary was one of four district schools to improve from a "C" to an "A" rating this year, along with Dwight D. Eisenhower K-8, Glade View Elementary, and West Gate Elementary.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to receive 2026 All-America City Award
cards.teaser: The City of Riviera Beach was selected as one of 10 communities nationwide to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, the only Florida city honored this year.
cards.body:
Riviera Beach has been named one of just 10 communities in the U.S. to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, making it the only Florida city selected for the honor this year. The award recognizes communities that bring residents, local government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges and create lasting change. The announcement was made during the National Civic League conference in Denver. Mayor Douglas Lawson called the recognition a proud moment for the city, stating that "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." Lawson credited a long-term effort to revitalize the city and improve quality of life for residents.

Riviera Beach's application highlighted several civic participation programs: the Riviera Beach Youth Council, which involves high school students in civic leadership; the Citizens Leadership Academy, a civic education initiative with a 98% completion rate; and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program, which provides mini-grants to help longtime homeowners make critical repairs. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for the honor, stating the award "belongs to all of us." The All-America City Award has been presented annually since 1949. The nine other award-winning cities are Chelsea, Massachusetts; Franklin, Tennessee; Harlingen, Texas; Montgomery, Alabama; Morrisville, North Carolina; Norfolk, Virginia; North Charleston, South Carolina; Roanoke, Virginia; and Woodburn, Oregon.

cards.headline: Juno Beach weighs costly fence replacement at JB-7 beach access after resident complaints
cards.teaser: Colony Condos residents say beachgoers are cutting through private property at the JB-7 public walkway since the town removed a fence in 2023 for safety reasons.
cards.body:
Residents at the Colony Condos in Juno Beach say people using the JB-7 public beach walkway are cutting through their private property since the town removed a fence in 2023 for safety reasons. With only bushes now separating the public access path from private land, Colony resident Lori Hill said the problem peaks in summer when beachgoers park in private spots and push through vegetation with coolers, fishing rods and lawn chairs. Hill said residents used to confront trespassers directly, but those encounters often turned hostile, so they now call police to handle the confrontations.

The dispute came before the Juno Beach Town Council at a recent meeting, where a town official noted the town is not obligated to install a fence. Vice Mayor Pro Tem DD Halpern suggested exploring a lower-cost solution such as a split rail fence combined with shrubs rather than a full replacement, which could cost thousands of dollars. Hill said residents hope the town will reinstall a fence to protect their landscaping and private parking. The council agreed to address the fence question during its budget discussions on July 15.

cards.headline: Saint Andrew's Scots football aims for state title after 10-2 season and district championship
cards.teaser: The Saint Andrew's Scots finished last season with a 10-2 record and a district title but fell in the second round of the playoffs.
cards.body:
The Saint Andrew's Scots football team is preparing for the 2026 fall season with a state title in their sights after finishing last year 10-2 with a district championship. Despite the strong regular season record, a second-round playoff exit left the team believing more was possible. Head coach Jimmy Robertson said most of the seniors are four-year players who came up through the middle school program, giving them familiarity with how the program operates. "Most of these seniors are four-year seniors. I mean, if not the majority of them came from the middle school as well. So they know how things are run. They had a lot of success in their career, and hopefully their senior year is the best season that we've had," Robertson said.

The Scots are tackling a more challenging schedule this fall to reach the next level. Senior Jack Williams said the team wanted to compete against stronger opponents to elevate the program. Senior Jack Whelche emphasized that playoff advancement, not regular season success, defines improvement. "A better year is just gonna be going farther in the playoffs. Obviously we wanna go undefeated in the season, but that doesn't matter if we keep losing in the second round of the playoffs," Whelche said. Senior Edmyer St. Jean said summer workouts provide daily motivation as the team works to break their previous record.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient speaks out after Anthem denies reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, was denied coverage for breast reconstruction surgery involving GalaFlex mesh less than 24 hours before the scheduled procedure.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago and underwent a full double bilateral mastectomy with planned reconstruction using GalaFlex surgical mesh. Less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield denied coverage for the procedure, citing in the denial letter that the surgery is considered "investigational" and "there is no or not enough proof it improves health." GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh that is FDA-approved for some uses in the body but not for breast reconstruction, making it an off-label, investigational and experimental treatment. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated that the product's "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Dr. Alicia Billington, Clark's plastic surgeon, uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and says the product gives patients fewer complications than other options. Despite Anthem's denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery a little more than a week ago after Billington found a mechanism to make it happen. An Anthem spokesperson said the company regularly reviews coverage policies to ensure they are based on medical evidence and aligned with treatment standards, but GalaFlex "does not currently meet the standards required for coverage." Clark still has the right to appeal. Last year, Cigna became the first and only major insurer to start approving GalaFlex for breast reconstruction following reporting on patient denials.

cards.headline: Boca Raton High School band to represent Florida at National Independence Day Parade
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton Community High School band will march in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade on July 4 at 10:30 a.m.
cards.body:
The Boca Raton Community High School band has earned an invitation to march in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade on July 4 at 10:30 a.m., representing Florida. The students will march a full mile along the National Mall from Constitution Avenue to Independence Avenue. Only bands nominated by state officials receive invitations to the prestigious event.

Junior Lola Cabezas said millions of people will be watching the parade. Senior Stephin Restivo said the team is focused on marching and timing so everyone can see what the Boca High band is capable of. Band Director Jenn Girdlestone said she has full confidence the students will put their best foot forward and represent the country well. Senior Lily Schaffer said making it to Washington, D.C. shows how much the program has grown. The parade will be streamed live on YouTube for those who want to watch from home.
